name: Spondee-Caldera
geological_features: Single massive caldera covering 40% of the surface
specific_features: Periodic mega-eruptions that reshape the entire surface
Microbial life that enters dormancy between eruption cycles
description: Spondee-Caldera is a small volcanic world dominated by a single enormous caldera that covers nearly half its surface, a wound in the crust so vast it is better described as a geological feature than a crater. The caldera floor is an active hell of sulfur geysers, lava lakes, and volcanic glass dune fields sculpted by toxic winds. The remaining surface is scarred badlands of cooled ejecta from past mega-eruptions, layered in patterns that record the planet's violent cyclical history.

The low gravity means eruption plumes escape easily into the upper atmosphere, sometimes achieving escape velocity and forming temporary debris rings around the planet. The toxic atmosphere thins dangerously at altitude but thickens in the caldera basin where volcanic gases pool in lethal concentrations. The visual effect during an eruption cycle is spectacular: fountains of magma arcing in the low gravity, falling slowly enough to cool into twisted sculptural forms before landing.

Microbial life persists here in one of the most extreme survival strategies known to science. During quiescent periods between mega-eruptions, thermophilic colonies bloom in the caldera's cooler margins, metabolizing sulfur compounds and reproducing rapidly. When eruption cycles begin, the colonies enter a spore-like dormancy state that can survive temperatures exceeding five hundred degrees and burial under meters of fresh lava. They have been doing this for billions of years, a life cycle measured in geological epochs.

The eruption cycle is accelerating according to long-term monitoring data, and xenobiologists fear the intervals between events may eventually become too short for the microbial colonies to complete their reproductive cycles. If so, Spondee-Caldera's unique extremophile ecosystem may be lost. Research teams maintain orbital stations to study the phenomenon, but the planet's hostility prevents any form of intervention. All they can do is watch and document what may be the slow extinction of life that has endured since the planet's formation.
